scope: Ten synthetic minimal deduction lines. Provider explanations do not classify claims; deterministic answer-key accuracy is tested separately.

cases.title: Room-category proportional reduction
cases.input:
Synthetic QA. Deduction Rs 8000: Surgeon and OT charges: proportionate reduction of 20% because chosen room rent was Rs 6,000 against eligible room rent Rs 4,800.
Applicable policy clause not supplied.
cases.answer_key: The description identifies a room-category ratio applied to associated charges. Request the actual clause, affected-item calculation and whether those charges vary by room. Neither the historical 2020 circular nor a ratio alone establishes that the reduction is prohibited.
cases.explanation: The deduction means the insurer will lower the claim by ₹8,000. This amount comes from a 20 % reduction applied to the surgeon’s and operating‑theatre (OT) fees because the hospital room chosen cost ₹6,000 per day, while the policy only allows a maximum (eligible) room rent of ₹4,800 per day. The excess room cost is not covered, so the related charges are reduced proportionally. The exact policy clause governing this reduction was not provided.
cases.review_note: Treats an unprovided room-rent clause and related-expense reduction as established coverage facts.

cases.title: Consumable item with unknown rider
cases.input:
Synthetic QA. Deduction Rs 1500: Non-medical consumables: gloves Rs 550, oxygen mask Rs 400, admission kit Rs 550. Deducted under excluded items; no rider review shown.
Applicable policy clause not supplied.
cases.answer_key: Exact items appear in different historical lists: gloves I.56, oxygen mask I.62, admission kit II.27. Those historical labels cannot decide present coverage. Request policy exclusion, consumable rider and any package/room inclusion before concluding recoverability.
cases.explanation:
The deduction is a Rs 1,500 charge for “non‑medical consumables.” It lists three items:

- Gloves – Rs 550  
- Oxygen mask – Rs 400  
- Admission kit – Rs 550  

These items are treated as “excluded items,” meaning the policy does not cover them, so their cost is subtracted from the claim. The note says no rider (policy add‑on) review is shown, and the specific policy clause that governs this exclusion was not provided.
cases.review_note: States that the policy does not cover the items although the applicable clause/rider is missing.

cases.title: Confirmed cataract benefit cap
cases.input:
Synthetic QA. Deduction Rs 4500: Cataract sub-limit: procedure bill Rs 54,500; eligible policy limit Rs 50,000 per eye; excess Rs 4,500.
Policy clause supplied: DEMO clause 4.2: cataract benefit is limited to Rs 50,000 per eye for this policy year; no prior utilization.. Calculation confirmed: true.
cases.answer_key: In this synthetic scenario the user confirms the applicable per-eye cap and the arithmetic: 54,500 minus 50,000 is 4,500. Likely valid is conditional, not an adjudication; policy version, utilization and riders still matter. The linked cataract post is only contextual, not evidence this fictional cap exists.
cases.explanation: The text says the cataract benefit is capped at ₹50,000 for each eye in the current policy year. The actual procedure cost is ₹54,500, which is ₹4,500 over the limit. Therefore a deduction of ₹4,500 is applied. The policy clause confirming this limit is needed for full verification.
cases.review_note: Correct cap and arithmetic; requests verification without asserting legal validity.

cases.title: Confirmed co-payment with calculation base
cases.input:
Synthetic QA. Deduction Rs 14500: Co-payment at 20% of the admissible amount Rs 72,500 = Rs 14,500; balance insurer liability Rs 58,000.
Policy clause supplied: DEMO schedule: 20% co-payment applies to each admissible hospitalization claim; no waiver or special network exemption.. Calculation confirmed: true.
cases.answer_key: Both clause applicability and calculation are expressly confirmed by the fixture user. The arithmetic 72,500 x 20% = 14,500 supports the conditional status. Public shortfall reports illustrate confusion about partial approval, not proof of co-pay terms.
cases.explanation:
The text shows how a hospital claim is reduced by a **co‑payment**.  
* **Admissible amount** – the total cost the insurer allows for the hospitalization (₹ 72,500).  
* **Co‑payment at 20 %** – the insured must pay 20 % of that amount, which is ₹ 14,500.  
* **Deduction** – the ₹ 14,500 the insured pays, subtracted from the claim.  
* **Insurer liability** – the remaining amount the insurer will pay, ₹ 58,000.  
The policy states that a 20 % co‑payment applies to every eligible hospital claim, with no waivers or network exceptions.
cases.review_note: Correct copay base/arithmetic and supplied term.

cases.title: Reasonable-and-customary reduction
cases.input:
Synthetic QA. Deduction Rs 12000: Consultant professional fee Rs 32,000 reduced to Rs 20,000 on reasonable and customary grounds; comparison data not enclosed.
Applicable policy clause not supplied.
cases.answer_key: The insurer label identifies the category but does not establish an evidence-based comparison, geographic benchmark or policy clause. Seek the reference data and line calculation. Do not characterize every reasonable-and-customary reduction as unlawful.
cases.explanation: The note records a claim deduction of ₹12,000. It says the consultant’s professional fee was originally ₹32,000, but the insurer reduced it to ₹20,000, citing “reasonable and customary” limits. No supporting comparison data was provided, and the specific policy clause that allows this adjustment was not included. This explanation only clarifies the terminology used.
cases.review_note: Attributes R&C reason and identifies missing comparison/wording.

cases.title: Package inclusion rather than consumable exclusion
cases.input:
Synthetic QA. Deduction Rs 2400: Surgical tape and gauze Rs 2,400 deducted as already included in the surgery package. Hospital bills the items separately and says they were outside the agreed package.
Applicable policy clause not supplied.
cases.answer_key: The operative reason is alleged package inclusion, despite names of consumable items. Compare agreed package and hospital bill to determine whether this is duplicate billing or an incorrect package assumption. Historical List III labels do not settle the dispute.
cases.explanation: The note says a deduction of ₹2,400 was made because the cost of surgical tape and gauze was claimed to be already covered in the surgery package. The hospital, however, billed those items separately and says they are not part of the package. No specific policy wording is provided to confirm whether this deduction is correct.
cases.review_note: Preserves disputed package inclusion and need for wording.

cases.title: Alleged unrelated investigation
cases.input:
Synthetic QA. Deduction Rs 3100: Thyroid profile and vitamin panel Rs 3,100 are not related to the admitted ankle injury. Treating doctor ordered them during the same admission.
Applicable policy clause not supplied.
cases.answer_key: Timing within an admission neither proves nor disproves medical relation. Request the specific terms and clinical basis and obtain the treating doctor explanation. The app must not independently diagnose or assert medical necessity.
cases.explanation: The note says a deduction of ₹3,100 was made because the thyroid‑profile and vitamin‑panel tests, costing ₹3,100, are considered unrelated to the ankle injury for which the patient was admitted. Although the attending doctor ordered these tests during the same hospital stay, the insurer views them as separate, non‑injury‑related expenses. The specific policy clause that governs such exclusions was not provided, so the exact rule applied cannot be identified.
cases.review_note: Attributes insurer position; does not diagnose clinical necessity.

cases.title: Blank deduction explanation
cases.input:
Synthetic QA. Deduction Rs 3250: Adjustment against final payable amount: Rs 3,250. Remarks: as per terms. Item-wise reason: —.
Applicable policy clause not supplied.
cases.answer_key: A numeric adjustment and generic terms label do not communicate the full item-specific reason and policy term. The correct next action is to ask for reasons; do not invent a consumables/co-pay/category explanation.
cases.explanation: The text says a deduction of ₹3,250 will be subtracted from the final amount you have to pay. It notes the deduction is “as per terms,” but does not give the specific reason or the policy clause that allows it. The exact clause from the insurance policy is missing, so you would need to refer to the policy wording for details.
cases.review_note: Incorrectly says the deduction reduces the amount the user has to pay instead of the insurer payment.

cases.title: Approved room rent must not override actual co-pay
cases.input:
Synthetic QA. Deduction Rs 12500: Room rent approved in full, with no deduction. Deduction shown below: co-payment 20% on Rs 62,500, amount Rs 12,500. The policy clause is not enclosed.
Applicable policy clause not supplied.
cases.answer_key: The room charge is explicitly approved; the actual deduction is co-pay. Confirming arithmetic without an applicable policy clause cannot make it likely valid. A first-keyword room-rent match loses the negation and misstates the reason.
cases.explanation: The text says a hospital stay charge of ₹62,500 was approved, but a 20 % co‑payment is applied, resulting in a deduction of ₹12,500. “Co‑payment” means the insured must pay that percentage of the bill; the insurer pays the rest. No other policy clause is provided, so the exact rule governing this deduction is missing.
cases.review_note: Identifies actual copay and missing clause; broad approved-charge phrasing should be more precise.

cases.title: Exhausted maternity allowance without the word sub-limit
cases.input:
Synthetic QA. Deduction Rs 22000: Maternity benefit ceiling Rs 50,000 for the policy year. Prior maternity payment Rs 30,000; remaining allowance Rs 20,000. Current bill Rs 42,000; excess deducted Rs 22,000.
Applicable policy clause not supplied.
cases.answer_key: A treatment-specific benefit ceiling is a sub-limit even when the exact label is absent. Verify policy wording, period and prior utilization. The post reference concerns a policy-period dispute and is contextual only; all maternity terms here are synthetic.
cases.explanation: The text says the policy limits maternity benefits to ₹50,000 per year. A previous claim of ₹30,000 has already been paid, leaving ₹20,000 of benefit remaining. A new hospital bill of ₹42,000 was submitted, but only the remaining ₹20,000 can be covered, so ₹22,000 is deducted (not paid). The specific policy clause that sets this limit was not provided, so the exact wording is needed for full clarification.
cases.review_note: Terminology only; no invented policy clause or classification change.
